The Trail of Tears. Between eighteen thirty-one and eighteen fifty, the catastrophic forced removal of Native American tribes, primarily the Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Seminole, occurred from their ancestral homelands in the southeastern United States to designated territories in present-day Oklahoma. Thousands died during the journey from disease, starvation, and exposure, making it one of the deadliest ethnic cleansings in American history and a defining tragedy of Indian removal policy.

The removal was authorized by the Indian Removal Act of eighteen thirty under President Andrew Jackson. The policy was built on the premise of "civilizing" and "concentrating" Native peoples away from expanding white settlements. The Cherokee removal took place between eighteen thirty-eight and eighteen thirty-nine. Over four thousand Cherokee died in winter conditions during the forced march from present-day North Carolina and Georgia to Indian Territory in Oklahoma, out of roughly sixteen thousand displaced.

The Creek War between eighteen thirteen and eighteen fourteen preceded removal and saw brutal conflict between factions. The Treaty of Fort Jackson in eighteen fourteen stripped the Creek Nation of millions of acres, setting the precedent for mass dispossession. Other nations were forcibly removed: the Choctaw between eighteen thirty-one and eighteen thirty-three with roughly four thousand deaths, the Chickasaw between eighteen thirty-seven and eighteen thirty-eight, the Seminole between eighteen thirty-eight and eighteen forty-two which was the most violent removal, and the Creek between eighteen thirty-four and eighteen thirty-seven.

The removals were justified by pseudo-legal treaties often imposed under duress or signed by unrepresentative factions. The Cherokee fought removal in court with the case Worcester v. Georgia in eighteen thirty-one, but were ignored by Jackson's administration. The destination, Indian Territory, was portrayed as permanent, but western expansion and the Oklahoma Land Run in eighteen eighty-nine soon invaded this refuge, repeating the cycle of dispossession.
